name: Example: Calculating a Moment of Inertia About a Perpendicular Axis Using Polar Coordinates
problem: Calculate the moment of inertia of a circular plate that occupies the region of a disk $D$ of radius $1\,\textrm{m}$ with mass density $\lambda(x, y) =2(x^2+y^2),$ measured in $\textrm{kg}/\textrm{m}^2,$ about a line perpendicular to the disk passing through a point on the circumference.
worked_solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line $l_M$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to $l_M$ is given by

$$
I_l = I_M + d^2M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and $I_M$ and $I_l$ are the moments of inertia about the lines $l_M$ and $l,$ respectively.

First, notice that the region $D$ can be expressed in polar coordinates as

$$
D = \big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi \big\}.
$$

Since the mass density is symmetric in $x$ and $y,$ $D$'s center of mass is at $(0,0).$ The mass density function, in polar coordinates, is given by $\lambda(r,\theta) = 2r^2.$

Next, we find the mass of the plate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}2{r}^{2}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{4}{|}_{0}^{1}\cdot \theta {|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =\pi \,\text{kg}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}2{r}^{2}\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{r}^{5}\,\text{d}r\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{r}^{6}{|}_{0}^{1}\cdot \theta {|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a line passing through a point on the circumference is

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}+{1}^{2}\cdot \pi  \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}+\pi  \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
